nameStory: Rock buttercup gets its name from its love of rocky, gravelly places where many other buttercups won't grow. The 'buttercup' part comes from the old belief that cows eating these golden flowers would produce richer, more yellow butter - though in reality, most buttercups are actually toxic to livestock!
description: Rock buttercup is a small, delicate wildflower that's easy to overlook in the buttercup family. It produces tiny pale yellow flowers that are much smaller and less showy than the bright golden blooms of its meadow-loving cousins. This low-growing annual typically reaches only 6-12 inches tall, with a somewhat scraggly appearance and deeply divided leaves that give it an almost ferny look.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale yellow flowers, much smaller than other buttercups - often less than 1/4 inch across with 5 delicate petals that may appear almost white in poor light

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are kidney-shaped with rounded lobes, while upper leaves are deeply cut into narrow segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small, branching annual that grows in a somewhat sprawling pattern, rarely over a foot tall with thin, weak stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Forms small clusters of tiny, shiny achenes (one-seeded fruits) that gleam like little brown beads when mature

habitat: Look for rock buttercup in disturbed rocky areas, gravel paths, thin soils around stone walls, and woodland edges with poor, gravelly soil. It thrives in spots where the soil is too thin or rocky for larger, more competitive plants. Often found in partially shaded areas where the ground stays somewhat moist but well-drained.

seasonality.spring: Emerges early and begins blooming in late spring, often while larger plants are still getting established. Fresh green leaves appear first in rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny pale yellow flowers opening throughout early to mid-summer. Seeds begin forming as flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Plants typically complete their lifecycle and die back by late summer, leaving behind scattered shiny seeds for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: Gone entirely - this annual plant survives winter only as seeds tucked into rocky crevices and gravelly soil.

funFact: Rock buttercup is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 13 times by naturalists - making it more elusive than many orchids and about as uncommon as finding a four-leaf clover in your backyard!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small-flowered buttercup, which grows in similar habitats and has nearly identical tiny pale flowers. The key difference is subtle: rock buttercup has hairy flower centers (receptacles) and shiny seeds, while small-flowered buttercup has smooth flower centers and duller seeds - you'll need a hand lens to be certain!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crowfoot' in some references, this has nothing to do with actual crow feet - the name refers to the deeply divided leaf shape that early botanists thought resembled a bird's foot. Many buttercups share this alternate 'crowfoot' name, which can be confusing for beginners.
compareHints: Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms. Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or the sprawling creeping buttercup, rock buttercup is delicate and annual, completing its entire life cycle in one growing season. Its preference for rocky, disturbed ground also sets it apart from water-loving spearworts or the rich-soil meadow species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
